prompt: What does caffeine block in your brain to fight fatigue?
funFact: Caffeine is shaped closely enough to sit in the same receptors as adenosine — without switching them on. The fatigue is still there; you just stop receiving the message.

prompt: What is "3-in-1" coffee?
options: An instant coffee, creamer and sugar sachet
funFact: It's how most Filipinos actually drink coffee — no shame in the sachet.

prompt: Which brewing method uses full immersion for about four minutes?
funFact: Heavy body, some sediment, and the hardest brewer to ruin.

prompt: A latte is built from two espresso shots and mostly what?
funFact: Two shots plus 240 ml steamed milk with about 1 cm of foam is the café's house default.

prompt: A coffee bean starts out as a seed inside what?
funFact: How you remove the fruit around the seed decides most of the final flavour.

prompt: Which grind size does espresso need?
funFact: Espresso only has about 25 seconds of contact time, so it needs the finest grind of any method.

prompt: Barako coffee comes from which of the four commercial coffee species?
funFact: Barako isn't a brand or roast level — it's a distinct species, and the Philippines is one of the few places that grows it commercially.

prompt: Which Philippine town saw the country's first coffee planted, in 1740?
funFact: A Spanish friar planted it — coffee reached the Philippines the same way it reached most producing countries: through empire.

prompt: Which brewer is the only one that actually makes real espresso?
funFact: 9 bars of pressure in 25 seconds — nothing else on the list reaches that, which is also why nothing else can make a real latte.

prompt: Which brew method needs the coarsest grind?
funFact: The longer water sits with the grounds, the coarser the grind needs to be — cold brew steeps for up to 18 hours.

prompt: About how long does caffeine take to reach peak effect?
funFact: Its half-life is about 5 hours, so a 3pm cup is still half in your system at 8pm.

prompt: For long-haul drivers, coffee is described in the deck as the closest thing to what?
funFact: Drowsy driving is measurably as dangerous as drunk driving, and two cups cuts incident rates on long hauls.

prompt: Coffeehouses in London earned what nickname in the 1600s?
funFact: For the price of a coffee, anyone could sit in on the day's news and debate it.

prompt: Robusta accounts for roughly what share of the world's coffee crop?
funFact: It's bold, rubbery, has roughly double Arabica's caffeine, and makes a great crema.

prompt: What ended the Philippines' run as a top coffee exporter in the 1880s?
funFact: The Philippines was the world's 4th largest coffee exporter until leaf rust wiped out the crop by 1889 — the crown never came back.

prompt: Which processing method dries the whole cherry in the sun, fruit still on, for weeks?
funFact: It's the riskier method to get right, but it produces heavy, sweet, berry-and-wine notes.

prompt: Which roast level sits at the lowest temperature and highest acidity?
funFact: Light roast isn't under-roasted — it's roasted to keep the origin's own flavour, which is where specialty coffee lives.

prompt: In the standard espresso shot recipe, how many grams of coffee go in?
funFact: 18 g in, 36 g out, in about 27 seconds — those three numbers are 90% of pulling a shot.

prompt: Which drink is built "upside down," with syrup and milk poured before the espresso shots?
funFact: Vanilla, milk, then shots poured on top, caramel drizzle to finish — which is why it's "marked," or macchiato.

prompt: The 2–4pm energy slump many office workers feel is described in the deck as what?
funFact: It's a real dip in the body clock, not weak will — coffee flattens it rather than fixing anything broken.

prompt: Roughly what daily caffeine amount is considered the safe adult limit?
funFact: That's roughly four cups a day.

prompt: Caffeine was on the Olympic Committee's banned substance list until what year?
funFact: Research links caffeine to a 2–4% endurance boost — enough that it was once treated as performance-enhancing.

prompt: Coffee reached which three regions as smuggled seedlings in the 1700s, becoming plantations?
funFact: Every coffee-producing country today traces its first seedlings to somebody's colonial project.

prompt: Excelsa, the rarest of the four commercial coffee species, makes up about what share of the world crop?
funFact: It's tart and dark-fruited; in the Philippines it's grown in Sulu and Basilan.

prompt: What actually determines how coarse or fine a coffee grind should be?
options: The altitude it was grown at
How long the water stays in contact with it
funFact: Espresso has about 25 seconds of contact time, so it needs a fine grind; cold brew steeps for 16 hours, so it needs a coarse one.

prompt: Which of these is true about dark roast coffee, according to the deck?
options: It has more caffeine than light roast
It has slightly less caffeine than light roast
It has exactly the same caffeine as any roast
funFact: Roasting burns off a small amount of caffeine, so dark roast is not "stronger" in caffeine — a common myth the deck sets out to kill.

prompt: According to the deck's milk-steaming rule, what temperature should steamed milk stop at?
funFact: Past 70°C, milk tastes scalded and won't foam again — the jug itself becomes too hot to hold at the right stopping point.

prompt: How many separate historical attempts to ban coffee does the deck list — all of which failed?
funFact: Mecca in 1511, Ottoman Istanbul, Sweden in 1746, and Prussia under Frederick the Great all tried and failed to outlaw it.

prompt: In what year did the phrase "coffee break" enter the language?
funFact: It started as an advertising slogan, not a workers' right.

prompt: Kapeng alamid is coffee made from beans that passed through which animal?
funFact: The beans are eaten and passed by a wild civet, then washed, dried, and sold for thousands a kilo.

prompt: Beyond the chemistry, what does the deck call coffee's most honest social function?
options: The most socially acceptable excuse to stop working and talk to someone
A substitute for alcohol at work events
funFact: Chemistry explains attention and mood — it doesn't explain why "let's grab coffee" is the easiest excuse there is to talk to someone.

prompt: Coffee first appeared as food, not a drink — how was it consumed in the 800s in the Ethiopian highlands?
funFact: Coffee started as food, chewed rather than brewed, centuries before Yemen's roasting and brewing.

prompt: How is an Americano built, according to the deck's recipe?
options: Two shots plus 180 ml hot water
One shot plus 120 ml hot water
Two shots plus 240 ml hot water
Three shots plus 90 ml hot water
funFact: Pouring the water first, under the crema, is how you keep the crema — if that matters to you.

prompt: How is a frappe built, according to the deck's recipe?
options: Two shots, 120 ml milk, a full cup of ice and sauce, blended
One shot, 60 ml milk, blended with sugar
Three shots poured over crushed ice
Two shots, no milk, shaken with ice
funFact: It's the best-selling drink in most Philippine cafés — cold drinks are where local cafés make their money.

prompt: About how many kilograms of coffee does the average person in Finland drink per year?
funFact: That's roughly four cups a day for every person, including babies — the Philippines drinks roughly 1 kg per person by comparison.

prompt: What everyday piece of technology was invented so researchers wouldn't climb the stairs to an empty coffee pot?
funFact: In 1991, the first webcam ever built was pointed at a coffee pot in Cambridge.

prompt: Composer Ludwig van Beethoven reportedly counted out exactly how many coffee beans per cup, every morning?
funFact: The deck calls him "the first documented coffee snob."

prompt: Coffee is the world's second most-traded commodity, after which one?
funFact: Around 2.25 billion cups of coffee are drunk every day worldwide.

prompt: Decaf coffee is not caffeine-free — about how much caffeine does a cup still carry?
funFact: "Decaffeinated" is not the same claim as "caffeine-free."

prompt: What's the correct way to judge when steamed milk is ready, according to the deck?
options: Swirl it so it pours glossy, like wet paint, not stiff bubbles
Spoon off the foam to check thickness
Time it to exactly 10 seconds regardless of sound
funFact: Stiff bubbles mean the milk was stretched too long — good microfoam pours like wet paint.
